match.reason: None of the bank points teaches deliberately varying paragraph length or shape for effect, such as a one-line paragraph for impact; they cover analytical paragraph structure, topic sentences, integrated paragraphs and argument development, which are related but different ideas.

note:

- Question b, wording: The stem says the paragraph 'refers back to the idea before it', and the right option repeats this as 'ties the short paragraph to the idea before it'. A student can match the wording without knowing how linking words work.

rejected.title: Varying paragraph structure
card: A paragraph groups sentences around one idea. Writers do not make every paragraph the same length or shape.
Long paragraph
gives room to explain, describe or build an argument step by step. Too many in a row can tire a reader.
Short paragraph
can be a single line. It can make a moment stand out, such as a shock, a turning point or a strong claim.
Even when the length changes, the text still needs to hold together. Linking words such as however or as a result, and repeated main ideas, connect one paragraph to the next.
rejected.remember: Vary paragraph length for emphasis, but keep the links so the text still flows.

a.q: A writer ends a long paragraph of calm description, then adds a one-line paragraph: "Then the lights went out." What is the main effect?
opts: It makes the sudden event stand out
It gives more detail about the setting
It gives room to explain the event step by step
It links two arguments with a connective
a.why: A very short paragraph after a long one creates a sharp break, so the event stands out. It adds no detail about the setting and does not explain anything step by step, since the line is only a few words long.
a.clue: Think about what a sudden change in length does to the reader's attention.

b.q: Priya writes an article with paragraphs of very different lengths. Her short paragraph opens with "Despite this," and refers back to the idea before it. Why does opening this way help the article?
opts: It ties the short paragraph to the idea before it
It lets the short paragraph skip having a main idea
It gives the short paragraph room to explain in detail
It makes every paragraph in the article the same length
b.why: "Despite this," is a linking word, and referring back repeats the earlier idea, so the short paragraph stays tied to the one before it and the text still flows. A linking word does not replace a main idea: every paragraph still groups sentences around one.
b.clue: Think about what the reader needs when paragraph lengths jump around.

Question b, other: The why says 'every paragraph still groups sentences around one [idea]', but the card says a short paragraph can be a single line. The plural 'sentences' could confuse students about one-line paragraphs.
